fields.meta_description: Build newsletter automation that drafts each issue, books sponsor slots, sends readers the sections they picked, and clears out quiet subscribers.
fields.h1: Build Newsletter Automation for Every Issue You Publish
fields.hero_description: Get newsletter automation that drafts each issue from your posts and links, then holds it for your editor to approve.
fields.features_heading: What Goes Into the App Behind Each Issue
fields.features_subheading: Each part handles one job between a published post and a subscriber's inbox.
fields.feature_1:
A draft issue built from the week's sources

The app pulls the posts you published and the links your team saved into one draft, in the section order you set. Prompt for a new source and Emergent changes the app.
fields.feature_2:
No send until the editor approves

The editor gets a Slack direct message with a link to the new issue. Edits made on the review screen go into it, and only an approved issue moves on to your email service.
fields.feature_3:
A booking calendar for sponsor slots

Sponsors pick an open slot on a form, and the app marks that issue date taken for everyone else. If the ad copy is missing at your deadline, the sponsor gets a reminder.
fields.feature_4:
Sections chosen by each reader

Readers pick topics on a preference form, and the app syncs those picks to your email service as tags through its API. Each issue carries only the sections a reader chose.
fields.feature_5:
A cleanup rule for readers who went quiet

You decide what quiet means, such as no clicks across a set number of issues. The app sends those readers one re-confirm email and sets anyone who ignores it to Inactive.
fields.feature_6:
Every subscriber in a database you own

Each subscriber record and sponsor booking lives in a database you own, and the app's runs have no task cap. The full code exports to your GitHub repository on paid plans.

fields.usecase_heading: What the App Handles Between Issues
fields.tab_content_1:
Every Thursday, a 9-item draft waits for Juniper

At 9 a.m. every Thursday, the app builds a draft of The Kettle Line from the 3 blog posts published that week and the 6 links the team saved in Slack. Juniper Ashdown, the editor, gets a direct message with the draft. Once she approves it, the app schedules the issue in the connected email service for Friday at 7 a.m.
fields.tab_content_2:
Copy due 5 days out, or the sponsor hears about it

Brackwater Tools books the primary sponsor slot in the Oct 30 issue of Trailhead Brief through the booking form, and the app marks it taken. The classified slot stays open. On Oct 25, 5 days before the issue, no ad copy has arrived, and the app emails the sponsor contact, Tobias Wren, an upload link.
fields.tab_content_3:
Her picks decide which 2 sections she reads

Odalys Ferrante picks Seasonal planting and Recipes on the Plot and Pantry preference form. The app saves her picks as tags in the email service, and her Friday issue carries those 2 sections. Tool reviews, the third section, stays out of her copy until she adds it on the same form.
fields.tab_content_4:
244 readers who went quiet are now Inactive

The Northgate Running Club newsletter flags 412 subscribers who clicked nothing in the last 12 issues and sends each one a re-confirm email. Of those, 168 click to stay on the list. After 14 days, the app moves the other 244 to Inactive. They stop getting issues, and their records stay in the database.

fields.howto_description: These 7 steps turn the way you already publish into newsletter automation, tested on last month's issues before it goes live.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List every source behind an issue
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pick an approver and a send time
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Describe the app in one prompt
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Connect your email service and Slack
fields.howto_step_1_des: Open your last 4 issues and note where each item came from, such as your blog or a Slack channel. Each source becomes an input the app reads before it builds the next issue.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Name one editor who approves each issue, then pick the send day and time. Leave a full day between the review and the send, which gives the editor room for changes.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write the prompt the way you would brief a new assistant editor, naming the sources and the approval rule. Emergent builds the app and its database from that prompt.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Add the API key for the email service you send from, so the app can save tags and schedule issues there. Connect Slack for the direct messages the editor gets.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 List the slots each issue sells
fields.howto_step_5_des: Name each sponsor slot and how many days before the send its ad copy is due. The booking form then shows only the issue dates where a slot is still open.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Set the rule for quiet readers
fields.howto_step_6_des: Choose how many issues without a click flag a reader, and how long the re-confirm email stays open. Review the first flagged list by hand before the app moves anyone to Inactive.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Run last month's issues through it
fields.howto_step_7_des: Give the app last month's posts and saved links, then compare what it builds with the issues you sent. Fix a missing source or the section order by prompting before the first live week.

faq_plan.a: Newsletter automation uses software tools and technologies to streamline and manage creating, sending, and tracking email newsletters. Beyond the send itself, it can cover drafting each issue from content you already publish and keeping the subscriber list current.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up newsletter automation?
faq_plan.a: Start with the steps you repeat for every issue, and give each one a trigger and an owner. With Emergent's AI automation builder, you describe those steps in a prompt and get a working app with its own database. Run one past issue through it as a dry run before the first real send.

faq_plan.q: What should newsletter automation software do besides schedule emails?
faq_plan.a: It should cover the work around the send: collecting content into a draft, routing it for approval, chasing sponsor deadlines, and keeping the list clean. A scheduler alone leaves an editor assembling each issue by hand. Check whether you can write your own rules or only pick templates. An app built on Emergent runs those rules with no task cap.

faq_plan.q: Can newsletter automation handle sponsor bookings?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if each sponsor slot is kept as a record tied to an issue date, with the sponsor and the copy deadline on it. A booking form that reads those records offers only open dates, and a reminder goes out when copy is late. If you pitch larger packages with custom pricing, proposal automation can draft and track those offers before a booking lands.

faq_plan.q: What should newsletter automation do when a reader unsubscribes?
faq_plan.a: It should take the reader off every list at once and cancel any issue already scheduled for them. For commercial email, the FTC's CAN-SPAM guide says to honor a recipient's opt-out request within 10 business days. The same guide says any opt-out mechanism you offer must be able to process opt-out requests for at least 30 days after you send your message.

faq_plan.q: Can newsletter automation send each reader different sections?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Store each reader's topic picks as tags in your email service, then build one issue whose sections show only to readers with the matching tag. Decide what a reader who picked nothing gets, such as every section, before the first send. Topic picks also sit in a database you own, where you can see which sections readers choose over time.

faq_plan.q: What should I ask readers before setting up newsletter automation?
faq_plan.a: Ask which topics they want most, with a short ranking survey that lists your current sections and a few new ideas. Each reader puts the topics in order, and the average rank shows which ones to lead with. Run it twice a year and compare the results with the links readers click.

faq_plan.q: Can newsletter automation pull posts from a blog feed?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if your blog publishes a feed or has an API. The app checks the feed on a schedule, picks up every post newer than the last issue, and adds each one with its title and link. Keep the editor's approval step, since a feed also carries posts you may not want in an issue.

faq_plan.q: Can newsletter automation handle reader submissions?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Give readers a submission form with a few fixed fields, such as a link and a one-line pitch. Each entry lands in a queue with a status the editor sets while building the issue. Emergent builds the form and the queue from a prompt, and you can add a field later by prompting.

faq_plan.q: How do I measure whether newsletter automation is working for readers?
faq_plan.a: Combine click data with a direct question about each issue. Clicks show which links got attention. A short likert questionnaire asks readers to rate a statement such as "This issue saves me time" on an agreement scale. Send it to a sample of readers twice a year and track the scores against open and click rates.

plan.angle: The top 10 for newsletter automation are glossaries and email-platform guides that stop at scheduling a send or a welcome series. This page shows the publishing work around a recurring issue that an app can run: a draft issue assembled from the week's posts and saved links and held for the editor, sponsor slots booked against issue dates with copy deadlines, sections chosen by each reader's topic picks, and a cleanup rule for readers who stopped clicking. Welcome series and timed sequences belong to drip campaign; scoring and cart recovery to marketing automation workflow.
